source.publisher: National Crime Agency (National Economic Crime Centre)
source.title: Red Alert: Exporting High Risk Goods

summary: The UK NECC, working through JMLIT and with OFSI and the FCDO, warns the financial sector and trade/logistics providers that Russia is using complex supply chains, alternative routes and third-country intermediaries to procure Western dual-use and other high-risk goods for its military despite sanctions. It cites UK sanctions on Turkey-, UAE- and Russia-based entities for exporting microelectronics, drones and dual-use goods, and lists 14 red flags covering diversionary destinations, overpayment, front companies with no web presence, letter-of-credit misuse, OFSI list similarity/co-location, and transshipment or last-minute rerouting of payments.

citations.quote: “High-risk goods” refers to Western items critical to Russian weapons systems and its military development. It includes, but is not exclusive to, dual-use goods.

Transactions involve a purported civil end-user, but research indicates customers with counterparties with connections with the military, such as an address that is a military facility or is co-located with military facilities in a country of concern.
A customer that significantly overpays for a Common High Priority list item, compared to known market prices.

Purchases under a letter of credit that are consigned to the issuing bank, not to the actual end user. In addition, supporting documents, such as a commercial invoice, do not list the actual end-user.
Transactions involving entities with little to no web presence, such as a website or a domain-based email account.
Transactions involving companies that are physically co-located, or have shared ownership, with an entity on the OFSI consolidated list.
Russia is deploying complex supply chains and alternative supply routes to acquire sanctioned products.
Transactions involving payments being made from entities located at known tranship ment points or involve atypical shipping routes to reach a destination.

extraction_notes: This is a UK NCA/OFSI Red Alert on sanctions circumvention, not a TBML-family document per se, so all four typology links were made in the 'sanctions' family rather than the label-sharing 'tbml' family (TBML007/TBML010) per the Knowledge Centre's family-preference rule. The 14 numbered red flags on pages 4-5 were consolidated into 8 representative indicators to keep citations well-supported rather than listing all 14; a reviewer may want the remaining flags (e.g. multiple similar suppliers, open lines of credit, phone country-code mismatch) added individually if the desk wants full coverage. Page-vs-printed-folio note: the printed page footer numbering runs one behind the PDF page index from page 2 onward, so PDF page 6 (where the transshipment red flag sits) is printed folio '5' on the page above it in sequence but the document's own page break placed it under the '=== PAGE 5 ===' marker for red flag 14 — verified against the '=== PAGE n ===' markers, not assumed; flagged here in case the printed_folio value needs correction on review. 'Russian oligarchs' is recorded as a category actor per the ActorType.CATEGORY rule since it describes a class, not a named entity. Jurisdictions list reflects countries explicitly implicated in sanctions-evasion routes or sanctioned entities (Turkey, UAE, China, Belarus, Serbia, Uzbekistan per page 3), plus Russia, Ukraine and the UK (issuer).
